builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Local Sparsity Enables Unsupervised LLM Safety Detection
summary: This method replaces supervised safety classifiers that require curated unsafe training data by performing anomaly detection over sparse autoencoder features, flagging inputs whose local activation support deviates from safe data. The cost is training or obtaining an SAE for each deployed model, building a safe-data reference distribution, and adding an activation-extraction plus masking pass to the inference pipeline; computation after masking is small, but the SAE itself must be hosted and kept in sync with the model. It can fail when unsafe inputs activate the same local supports as safe data, when the linear representation hypothesis or SAE quality is poor for a given model, and when attack distributions drift far from anything the 1% calibration set represents.
rationale: It is implementable on a single GPU with existing open SAEs and addresses a real production gap (novel attack detection without unsafe training data), but detection quality is model- and dataset-dependent, so workload-specific validation is required before adoption.
technique: Locally masked SAE-based unsupervised safety detection

claims.statement: This method replaces supervised safety classifiers that require curated unsafe training data by performing anomaly detection over sparse autoencoder features, flagging inputs whose local activation support deviates from safe data. The cost is training or obtaining an SAE for each deployed model, building a safe-data reference distribution, and adding an activation-extraction plus masking pass to the inference pipeline; computation after masking is small, but the SAE itself must be hosted and kept in sync with the model. It can fail when unsafe inputs activate the same local supports as safe data, when the linear representation hypothesis or SAE quality is poor for a given model, and when attack distributions drift far from anything the 1% calibration set represents.
With only 1% out-of-distribution data for calibration, locally sparse methods achieve near-optimal detection performance while using only 1-2% of SAE neurons for computation.
